Chapter 9: Building a Future—Policy, Progress, and the Limits of Reform
As the movement grew and evolved, something shifted. Instead of just taking to the streets, the real challenge became clear: how do you transform raw outrage into real, lasting change?
Suddenly, meetings with lawmakers, city officials, and community leaders were popping up all over. Words like “defund,” “invest,” and “transform” started showing up everywhere—from city council speeches to social media feeds. The conversation was finally breaking into the mainstream.
And for a while, it actually felt like the world was paying attention. Some wins came surprisingly fast. Cities promised to review police practices, invest more in mental health, and set up civilian oversight boards. There was this sense that doors were opening—maybe, just maybe, things were starting to change.
But change, as it turned out, wasn’t that simple. Progress moved in fits and starts. For every promise made, a few seemed to quietly fade away. Old habits—especially the ones that ran deep—were tough to break.
Take one organizer who’d spent years pushing for justice. She found herself staring at a wall of frustration, watching politicians offer supportive words, but not much else. That’s when it hit her: reform alone wasn’t going to cut it. The roots of injustice went way deeper than a new policy or two. Real change? That would mean rethinking our values from the ground up.
Even so, there were bright spots. Young people—fired up by the movement—ran for office, and some even won. Community groups rolled up their sleeves and built brand new institutions: schools, clinics, mutual aid networks, all grounded in their own values.
This work? Most of it happened quietly, behind the scenes. It wasn’t flashy, but it was real.
The movement learned to savor every small win, to find moments of joy even when the dream felt far away. Change was possible. But it was clear—it would take time, grit, and a willingness to imagine something radically different.
In the end, the fight for justice wasn’t a sprint. It was a marathon. The work would keep going, picked up by new voices, new leaders, and new dreams.
